title: How to Order Currywurst in Berlin - FAQ
subtitle: Skin or no skin, heat, sides, and the words to say at the counter.

items.q: What does mit Darm and ohne Darm mean?
items.a: Darm means casing. **Mit Darm** is a sausage in a natural pork casing that snaps when you bite it. **Ohne Darm** has no casing, so it is softer, paler and smoother.

items.q: Which is the original Berlin currywurst, with or without skin?
items.a: **Ohne Darm.** Curry 36 says the sausage Berlin used for currywurst in the 1950s was a scalded sausage without casing, and that the version with casing came later.

items.q: How do I order a currywurst in German?
items.a: Say the sausage, the heat and the side: **"Einmal Currywurst ohne Darm, scharf, mit Pommes rot-weiß, bitte."** Add **"zum Mitnehmen"** if you want it to go.
Not by default. The house normal is mild. Ask for **scharf** or **extra scharf** if you want heat, and start one step lower than you think at a stand known for spice.
Fries with **ketchup and mayonnaise**, red and white. Some Berliners call it **Pommes Schranke**, after the red and white barrier.

items.q: Where can I get currywurst ohne Darm in Berlin?
items.a: **Konnopke's Imbiss** under the U2 viaduct on Schönhauser Allee sells only ohne Darm. Its site lists Tuesday to Friday 11:00 to 18:00 and Saturday 12:00 to 18:00, closed Sunday and Monday. **Curry 36** serves both kinds.
Berlin credits **Herta Heuwer**, who served her sauce at her stand on Kantstraße in Charlottenburg on **4 September 1949**. A plaque marks the spot. Duisburg has since claimed an earlier version.
